Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 37?
Supporting homeownership is an important strategy for promoting economic security and wealth building. However, it is unclear whether Prop. 37 would meaningfully help “middle class” Californians who face the greatest barriers to homeownership to afford a home.
As Prop. 37 would be financed through revenue bonds — which do not require voter approval — the program proposed by this initiative could have been enacted legislatively or a comparable program could have been established by the California Finance Housing Agency. Prop. 37 is a citizens’ initiative spearheaded by former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg.
What Would Prop. 37 Do?
The Middle Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf) would direct the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to establish a middle-class homebuyer downpayment assistance program, funded with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. The new program would:
Provide up to 17% of the purchase price toward the down payment , which could only be used to purchase new homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser.
Require the buyer to put down at least 3% of the purchase price toward the down payment. Combined with the 17% state downpayment assistance, this would reach 20% of the home’s purchase price and eliminates the need for private mortgage insurance. A conventional first mortgage would cover the remaining amount.
Require the downpayment assistance to be provided as a loan, not a grant, which recipients are likely to pay back monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage . This would be in addition to the homebuyer’s monthly payments on their conventional first mortgage.
Allow applicants to have incomes up to 200% of the Area Median Income (AMI) , which varies by region.
Cap the maximum home purchase price at roughly $1 million to $1.5 million, depending on the county and other factors. This is equivalent to a $170,000-$255,000 downpayment assistance cap per home.
Not require applicants to be first-time or first-generation home buyers , nor would recipients owe the state any equity gained in their home. These are requirements of comparable state downpayment assistance programs the state currently operates.
Allow home builders to become “qualified builders,” and have their developments automatically qualify for the program if they meet specified labor and enforcement standards.
How Would Income Eligibility for Prop. 37’s Downpayment Assistance Vary Across California Counties?
Prop. 37 would make a broad group of Californians eligible for downpayment assistance by allowing family incomes not exceeding 200% of Area Median Income (AMI) to qualify, a threshold that extends well beyond established downpayment assistance programs.
AMI represents the midpoint of family incomes in a specific area, adjusted for household size. In other words, half of households in an area have incomes that exceed 100% AMI and half have incomes below that level, so 200% AMI is roughly double what a typical family makes in the area. The limit is tied to local incomes, so whether a family income would qualify for Prop. 37’s downpayment assistance would vary significantly across California.
For example, a Budget Center analysis of Census Bureau data shows that a family of four earning up to $166,800 annually in Madera County or up to $375,800 annually in Santa Clara County could each qualify for assistance. However, the final dollar amounts would be set by CalHFA if Prop. 37 is approved by voters.
How Is Prop. 37 Different from California’s Existing Downpayment Assistance Programs?
California operates several (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/index.htm) statewide homeownership programs through CalHFA, but Prop. 37 would take a different approach that could hit family budgets harder, as participants are likely to pay back the downpayment assistance monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage.
For example, CalHFA’s MyHome Assistance Program (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/myhome.htm) and the Dream for All Shared Appreciation Loan (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/dream/) program both provide downpayment assistance through deferred “silent second (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/myaccount/faqs.htm)” loans (also known as silent second mortgages). MyHome charges 1% simple interest on the assistance; Dream for All accrues no interest, but requires a 15% or 20% share of the home’s appreciation to go to the state. Under both programs, nothing is due on these silent second mortgages until the homeowner sells, refinances, or pays off the first mortgage. This ensures that the downpayment assistance doesn’t compete with the first mortgage, groceries, utility bills, or other basic needs in a family’s monthly budget.
Prop. 37’s approach is likely to require monthly payments. This is because CalHFA would issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, and by law those bonds must be repaid from the proceeds of the program itself — meaning the principal and interest of the second mortgages CalHFA issues. The second mortgages would need to generate steady, ongoing revenue to pay the debt from the revenue bonds. Language in the measure also states “a borrower may request a temporary hardship deferral of monthly interest payments on its middle-class homeownership loan,” further alluding to its intended structure.

Under Prop. 37, the second mortgage payment could also likely carry higher interest rates above conventional first mortgage rates. Although the measure states the intent to provide below-market downpayment assistance financing, it doesn’t guarantee it. The interest rate on the second mortgages would ultimately depend on the terms under which the bonds are issued and market conditions at the time of implementation, which are largely outside CalHFA’s control.
Revenue bonds that finance second mortgages are inherently riskier for investors because if a homeowner defaults, the first mortgage gets repaid before the second, leaving the bond investors more exposed to loss. Investors may therefore require a higher return to compensate for that additional risk, which could increase the interest rate on the second mortgage. This means Prop. 37’s second mortgage rate could land above the roughly 6.5% conventional first-mortgage rates buyers already face today. CalHFA wouldn’t set the actual rate or terms on the second mortgage until implementation, so the interest rate cannot be known before voters decide on Prop. 37.
Ultimately, while Prop. 37 could help get homebuyers to a 20% downpayment to avoid private mortgage insurance, the monthly repayment costs for the second mortgage could erode much of the benefit the downpayment assistance was meant to provide.
Would Prop. 37 Reach “Middle-Class” Californians Facing the Greatest Barriers to Homeownership?
Prop. 37 would make a broad range of households eligible for downpayment assistance, but income eligibility alone does not determine who can realistically purchase a home. Racial and ethnic disparities in income (https://www.ppic.org/publication/income-inequality-in-california/#:~:text=Overall%2C%20the%20highest,without%20college%20degrees.), wealth (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/#:~:text=Wealth%20gaps%20by%20race%20and%20ethnicity%20are%20large.), credit access (https://www.epi.org/publication/chasing-the-dream-of-equity/#:~:text=Despite%20the%20bill%E2%80%99s%20intention%20to%20expand%20credit%20access%2C%20Black%20applicants%20are%20consistently%20more%20likely%20to%20be%20denied%20loans%20than%20applicants%20from%20other%20racial%20groups%20(), and housing affordability (https://www.car.org/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/HAI2025byEthnicity#:~:text=Meanwhile%2C%20only%2011%20percent%20of%20Black%20households%20and%2011%20percent%20of%20Hispanic/Latino%20households%20had%20the%20same%20ability.) mean that not all eligible families across California may be positioned to benefit from the program as proposed.
Prop. 37 would require the buyer to put down at least 3% of the purchase price, which would still be unattainable for many Californians. For example:
A house that costs $500,000 would require a 3% down payment of $15,000.
A house that costs $700,000 would require a 3% down payment of $21,000.
These upfront costs could be out of reach for many families, with the result that Prop. 37’s assistance could largely benefit families with incomes toward the higher end of the eligibility range. According to the Public Policy Institute of California, the median amount in Californians’ checking and savings accounts was just over $18,000 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/0525ttr-appendix.pdf) in 2025 dollars. This means that a 3% down payment could still almost or entirely clear out most or all of what an average family has in checkings and savings.
Prop. 37 could also reinforce economic, racial, and ethnic inequities in homeownership. The measure is intended to help “middle class” Californians, roughly defined as those with incomes between 80% to 200% AMI. White families are overrepresented among middle- and upper-middle-income Californians (46%), compared to their share of all California families (42%).
In contrast, Black and Latinx families are underrepresented in this “middle class” income range. This means that white families could disproportionately benefit from this program — even though white households already make up the largest share of homeowners (https://www.ppic.org/blog/californias-renters/#:~:text=Within%20the%20state,a%20college%20degree.) in the state, while Black and Latinx renter households face disproportionately high housing costs (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CHP_State-Housing-Needs-Report-2025.pdf).
Prop. 37 does not require applicants to be first-time or first-generation home buyers, further exacerbating equity concerns. Black and brown communities have been historically excluded from building wealth (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/) and accumulating assets, making the barrier to entering the housing market even more pronounced. Families of color face occupational segregation (https://www.americanprogress.org/article/occupational-segregation-in-america/) that pushes them into lower-paying jobs. They are also less likely to inherit generational wealth (https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/p/2021-12-17-inheritances-by-race/), and are more likely to be renters. (https://www.ppic.org/blog/californias-renters/#:~:text=Within%20the%20state,a%20college%20degree.) These factors make it substantially more difficult to save for a down payment, even at similar income levels. Additionally, data limitations often mask significant disparities in homeownership (https://www.urban.org/urban-wire/why-does-homeownership-vary-so-widely-within-aapi-community) access across racial and ethnic groups, especially among Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander Californians.
Could Prop. 37 Encourage Sprawl and Harm the Environment?
By restricting downpayment assistance to newly built homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, Prop. 37 could push more “middle-class” housing onto land that’s not well suited for housing. Much of the land in California best suited for housing has already been developed (https://shou.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2025-02/recent-leg-actions-factsheet-updated-feb-2025_0.pdf), leaving remaining areas that are often far from job centers, prone to wildfire,environmentally sensitive, or important for agriculture.
While existing state down payment assistance programs are not immune to these concerns because they can also be used to purchase new homes, Prop. 37 goes further by limiting assistance exclusively to newly constructed homes. As a result, Prop. 37 could further direct “middle-class” housing demand toward suburban and exurban areas. This is a critical deviation from infill development — building on denser, already developed land — which has been the focus of state affordable housing and environmental efforts.
This pattern of building housing on the periphery of cities (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2936977/#:~:text=IN%20THE%20LAST,a%20city%2C%20is) is known as urban sprawl (https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf) and carries various environmental and equity considerations. Development in more suburban and inland areas can push Californians further from job centers, increasing their commute times and making it difficult to travel without a car (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2936977/#:~:text=People%20who%20live%20in%20large%20metropolitan%20areas%20often%20find%20it%20difficult%20to%20travel%20even%20short%20distances%20without%20using%20an%20automobile%2C%20because%20of%20the%20remoteness%20of%20residential%20areas%20and%20inadequate%20availability%20of%20mass%20transit%2C%20walkways%2C%20or%20bike%20paths). It may also encourage development in areas on the outskirts of cities that may cause new homes to infringe upon natural habitats and important agricultural lands (https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf), especially in areas like the Central Valley. Sprawl can also lead to divestment from urban areas (http://urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf), which are often composed of communities of color, and concentrate investment in higher-income, suburban neighborhoods, further exacerbating racial and income inequality across the state.
What Other Homeownership Costs Could Come with Prop. 37’s New-Construction Requirement?
Prop. 37’s new construction requirement could steer homebuyers toward housing with higher out-of-pocket costs on top of their monthly mortgage payments. Unlike existing state down payment assistance programs, which can be used to purchase both new and existing homes, Prop. 37 would limit assistance to newly constructed homes. New construction homes are more likely to come with homeowners association (HOA) dues, Mello-Roos assessments, and home insurance challenges.
HOA fees are far more common in new homes as nearly 70% of newly built homes (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-housing-hoa-fees/) listed for sale nationally in 2024 were subject to HOA dues, compared with about 38% of existing homes. In California, more than a third of residents live in an HOA — including about 65% of all California homeowners. The average monthly fee is $280 (https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2025/09/condo-hoa-fees.html), and fees can rise up to 20% annually without a homeowner vote under current state law.
New construction in undeveloped areas of California also often comes with Mello-Roos (https://www.treasurer.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-10/2023_1.pdf) special tax assessments, which fund infrastructure like roads, schools, and utilities in newly developed areas and are layered on top of regular property taxes — typically adding another monthly fee to new-build homes for years.
California’s home insurance market also compounds the problem. Some state insurers have stopped providing coverage in many of the wildfire-prone areas (https://calmatters.org/housing/2023/05/state-farm-california-insurance/#:~:text=%E2%80%9CA%20lot%20of%20

other%20insurers%20have%20stopped%20selling%2C%E2%80%9D%20said%20Amy%20Bach%2C%20executive%20director%20of%20United%20Policyholders%2C%20a%20consumer%20group.%20%E2%80%9CIf%20you%20talk%20to%20an%20agent%20or%20broker%20today%2C%20they%E2%80%99re%20going%20to%20tell%20you%20it%20can%20be%20pretty%20hard%20to%20find%20insurance%E2%80%9D%20outside%20of%20the%20FAIR%20plan%2C%20Bach%20said.%C2%A0) where new homes are being built which has statewide ramifications. California’s state-run insurer of last resort, known as the FAIR Plan, is likely to be overburdened (https://calmatters.org/housing/2023/05/state-farm-california-insurance/#:~:text=As%20the%20risk%20of%20catastrophic%20wildfire%20ramps%20up%20across%20California%2C%20that%20risk%20falls%20disproportionately%20on%20the%20FAIR%20Plan.) to the extent that more insurers drop coverage across the state.
While home insurance challenges are not unique to Prop. 37, they remain acute in the wildland-urban interface — where almost 45% of the houses built in California have been located (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/01/ca-wui-housing-policy/#:~:text=Between%201990%20and,in%20the%20state.) over the last 30 years. Though these areas tend to have less expensive real estate (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/01/ca-wui-housing-policy/#:~:text=%E2%80%9CPeople%20are%20looking%20to%20the%20(wildland%2Durban%20interface)%20as%20one%20of%20the%20only%20places%20that%20has%20capacity%20for%20housing%2C%E2%80%9D%20she%20said.%20Though%20the%20wildland%2Durban%20interface%20includes%20toney%20enclaves%20of%20wealth%20like%20Pacific%20Palisades%2C%20it%20also%20features%20some%20of%20the%20more%20affordable%20real%20estate%20left%20in%20the%20state.), they are also particularly susceptible to wildfires. That exposure could mean higher premiums, more difficulty securing a loan, or dependence on the FAIR Plan, driving additional costs on top of the repayments of Prop. 37.
Altogether, these compounding factors could undercut the affordability gains the measure is purported to provide for Californians. As a result, the benefits of Prop. 37 may skew toward eligible families with greater financial resources who were already better positioned to cover the costs of homeownership.
Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 37?
There have been some official supporters (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_37,_Second_Mortgage_Homebuyer_Program_and_Revenue_Bond_Initiative_(2026)#google_vignette:~:text=Who%20supports%20and%20opposes%20the%20initiative%3F) of the initiative, but no official opponents as of mid-summer 2026. Former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Robert Hertzberg is the primary sponsor and a supporter of this proposition. Hertzberg has stated the main goal of the measure is to allow working families and their children to build wealth and remain in California (https://www.planningreport.com/2025/10/01/keeping-our-children-california-hertzberg-middle-class-homeownership-act).
Various carpentry-focused unions and realty organizations — like the California Association of Realtors and the Northern California Carpenters Regional Council — have also expressed support for the measure. Gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra has also expressed support for this measure.

Various carpentry-focused unions and realty organizations — like the California Association of Realtors and the Northern California Carpenters Regional Council — have also expressed support for the measure. Gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra has also expressed support for this measure.

other%20insurers%20have%20stopped%20selling%2C%E2%80%9D%20said%20Amy%20Bach%2C%20executive%20director%20of%20United%20Policyholders%2C%20a%20consumer%20group.%20%E2%80%9CIf%20you%20talk%20to%20an%20agent%20or%20broker%20today%2C%20they%E2%80%99re%20going%20to%20tell%20you%20it%20can%20be%20pretty%20hard%20to%20find%20insurance%E2%80%9D%20outside%20of%20the%20FAIR%20plan%2C%20Bach%20said.%C2%A0) where new homes are being built which has statewide ramifications. California’s state-run insurer of last resort, known as the FAIR Plan, is likely to be overburdened (https://calmatters.org/housing/2023/05/state-farm-california-insurance/#:~:text=As%20the%20risk%20of%20catastrophic%20wildfire%20ramps%20up%20across%20California%2C%20that%20risk%20falls%20disproportionately%20on%20the%20FAIR%20Plan.) to the extent that more insurers drop coverage across the state.
While home insurance challenges are not unique to Prop. 37, they remain acute in the wildland-urban interface — where almost 45% of the houses built in California have been located (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/01/ca-wui-housing-policy/#:~:text=Between%201990%20and,in%20the%20state.) over the last 30 years. Though these areas tend to have less expensive real estate (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/01/ca-wui-housing-policy/#:~:text=%E2%80%9CPeople%20are%20looking%20to%20the%20(wildland%2Durban%20interface)%20as%20one%20of%20the%20only%20places%20that%20has%20capacity%20for%20housing%2C%E2%80%9D%20she%20said.%20Though%20the%20wildland%2Durban%20interface%20includes%20toney%20enclaves%20of%20wealth%20like%20Pacific%20Palisades%2C%20it%20also%20features%20some%20of%20the%20more%20affordable%20real%20estate%20left%20in%20the%20state.), they are also particularly susceptible to wildfires. That exposure could mean higher premiums, more difficulty securing a loan, or dependence on the FAIR Plan, driving additional costs on top of the repayments of Prop. 37.
Altogether, these compounding factors could undercut the affordability gains the measure is purported to provide for Californians. As a result, the benefits of Prop. 37 may skew toward eligible families with greater financial resources who were already better positioned to cover the costs of homeownership.
Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 37?
There have been some official supporters (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_37,_Second_Mortgage_Homebuyer_Program_and_Revenue_Bond_Initiative_(2026)#google_vignette:~:text=Who%20supports%20and%20opposes%20the%20initiative%3F) of the initiative, but no official opponents as of mid-summer 2026. Former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Robert Hertzberg is the primary sponsor and a supporter of this proposition. Hertzberg has stated the main goal of the measure is to allow working families and their children to build wealth and remain in California (https://www.planningreport.com/2025/10/01/keeping-our-children-california-hertzberg-middle-class-homeownership-act).
Various carpentry-focused unions and realty organizations — like the California Association of Realtors and the Northern California Carpenters Regional Council — have also expressed support for the measure. Gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra has also expressed support for this measure.

- Is supported across the political spectrum

The downside is bounded; the upside (potentially 60,000-1.8 million buyers helped, ~190,000 new homes) is significant in a state with a severe housing shortage and homeownership crisis.

I'll answer "yes."

3. Does it help people? Yes, potentially many families — voluntarily.

Weighing bounded downside vs. meaningful upside, plus broad support from credible housing policy voices (SPUR, YIMBY cautiously, CalMatters neutral), "yes" is the better vote.

# California’s Proposition 37 would let buyers put 3% down on a new home, with a state loan covering the other 17%
Proposition 37 would let CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers of newly built homes up to 17% of the price, so they can put 3% down.
...
Prop 37, the "California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026," is an initiative statute placed on the ballot by petition.
It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide and the best-polling of them: 61% yes to 35% no in PPIC's September survey.
No argument against it was filed, no opposition committee exists, and its Yes side reports $30.9 million from top donors, led by the state's Realtors, the carpenters' unions and the Brin-and-Doerr-funded Building a Better California.
Governor Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra and the California Democratic Party support it, the California Republican Party is neutral, and the editorial boards split two to two.
...
## Proposition 37's Yes side reports $30.9 million from Realtors, carpenters and Building a Better California with no opposition committee:
The Fair Political Practices Commission's top-contributor list, updated October 14, shows $30.9 million in support of Prop 37 across two committees and no opposition committee large enough to appear.
...
## Proposition 37 leads 61% to 35% with Newsom, Becerra and Democrats in support and editorial boards split:
PPIC's September survey of likely voters, fielded September 4–10, found 61% yes, 35% no

https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/prop-37-california-down-payment-assistance-explained/
Proposition 37 on the Nov. 3 ballot would allow the state to amass a $25 billion down payment assistance program for middle-class households.
...
The ballot measure would allow qualified prospective homebuyers to borrow up to 17% of the sales price of a new home, contributing 3% of the down payment from their own funds.
The program would not be funded by taxpayers, but instead by the interest charged to borrowers on their down payment loans, also referred to as second mortgages.
The measure has garnered widespread support, including from Gov.
Gavin Newsom, statewide unions and mayors from Santa Monica to San José.
'Prop.
37 is a historic opportunity to expand homeownership opportunities for generations of working families — at zero cost or risk to taxpayers,' Newsom said in a statement.
...
While Proposition 37 has little opposition, and is supported by unions, chambers of commerce and organizations representing builders, the League of Women Voters opposes the ballot measure, concerned it would saddle residents with too much debt and that the terms of these loans are opaque, the details worked out only after the vote.
...
One of the biggest financial backers of the measure is the political nonprofit Building a Better California, which has been fighting the billionaire's tax with help from wealthy donors, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin.

3. What's on California's ballot in the 2026 midterm election? A voter's guide to the statewide races

# What's on California's ballot in the 2026 midterm election? A voter's guide to the statewide races
## Governor
Becerra's most notable endorsements include Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris.
...
## Proposition 2: Increases California's rainy day fund
Supporters, including Newsom and Becerra, say the measure would better protect funding for education, healthcare and public safety during economic downturns.
...
## Proposition 37: Creates a loan program for middle-income homebuyers
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a state homebuying assistance program for eligible middle-income Californians purchasing newly built homes.
The program would provide fixed-rate loans covering up to 17% of a qualifying home's purchase price.
Eligible buyers would have to meet income requirements, occupy the home as their residence and make a down payment of at least 3%.
A yes vote would establish the program and authorize the bonds.
A no vote would prevent the state from being required to create it.
The measure's proponents say it would make homeownership more accessible without directly relying on taxpayer-funded bond repayments.
The bonds would be repaid through borrowers' mortgage payments.

Now I have a comprehensive picture. Let me summarize the key considerations:

**Arguments FOR Prop 37 (Yes):**
1. **No direct taxpayer cost** - Revenue bonds repaid by borrowers, not taxpayers. LAO confirms "no direct state or local costs."
2. **Addresses a real barrier** - Down payment is the biggest hurdle to homeownership in California. A 20% down payment on a median ~$900K home is ~$180K.
3. **Tied to new construction** - Unlike most down payment assistance (which just increases demand for fixed stock and drives up prices), this one incentivizes new supply. SF Chronicle: "Most down-payment assistance programs for home buyers drive up housing costs. Prop 37 is different."
4. **Broad bipartisan support** - Gov. Newsom, State Treasurer Fiona Ma, Controller Malia Cohen, unions (Carpenters, Nurses, Teachers), chambers of commerce, builders, veterans groups, California Association of Realtors, YIMBY Action (cautiously supportive).
5. **Consumer protections** - Fixed-rate loans, "as low as possible" rates, annual audits, no prepayment penalty, no PMI needed.
6. **SPUR recommends Yes** - respected urban policy think tank.
7. **SF Chronicle Editorial Board endorses Yes.**
8. **Construction defect reform** - could help revive condo construction ("missing middle" housing).
9. Polls suggest it's popular; no formal opposition campaign.
10. CalMatters notes ~90% of California renters would be income-eligible.

**Arguments AGAINST Prop 37 (No):**
1. **League of Women Voters of California opposes** - second mortgage adds monthly debt burden; terms unknown before approval (interest rate, term); could help buy a home "without making it affordable to keep."
2. **Equity concerns** - No priority for first-time/first-generation buyers; doesn't exclude current/former homeowners; income cap up to 200% AMI (~$300K-$400K+ in some areas) could benefit wealthier households; could reinforce racial gaps (white/Asian households overrepresented in eligibility range). SPUR and Budget Center both note this.
3. **Interest rate risk** - Second mortgages are riskier for investors (subordinate to first mortgage, no state or Fannie/Freddie guarantee), so rates could be above conventional mortgage rates (~6.5%), eroding the benefit. PPIC analysis: less than 40% of eligible renters could afford the higher monthly payments on an entry-level home.
4. **Could inflate prices** - If builders can't respond fast enough, more demand chases limited new-home supply, raising prices (California YIMBY concern: "instead of 10 people bidding... now there's 12 people bidding on the same house"). San Diego U-T and SLO Tribune editorials argue demand-side subsidy can't fix a supply problem.
5. **Unknown investor demand** - Uncertain whether investors will buy $25B in these risky revenue bonds; Hertzberg wouldn't name any committed buyers.
6. **Sprawl/environmental concerns** - Restricting to new construction could push development to outskirts, wildfire-prone areas; new homes often come with HOA fees, Mello-Roos taxes, and insurance challenges.
7. **Most renters couldn't afford even the cheapest new homes** even with help (PPIC).
8. **Editorial opposition**: Sacramento Bee ("risky $25 billion housing experiment"), Santa Cruz Sentinel, San Diego Union-Tribune, SLO Tribune/East Bay Times (reject Props 1 and 37).
9. **Policy details deferred** - Terms set after the vote; the program could have been enacted legislatively (vanity project concern).
10. **It's a big bet on an unproven mechanism** - essentially making the state one of the largest mortgage brokers (DeMaio's concern about government involvement).

Editorial scoreboard on Prop 37:
- Yes: SF Chronicle Editorial Board, SPUR
- No: Sacramento Bee, Santa Cruz Sentinel, San Diego Union-Tribune, SLO Tribune, East Bay Times, League of Women Voters
- Neutral/explanatory: LA Times (news coverage), CalMatters (explainer with critical angles)

Now, I need to make a judgment call. The question asks me to decide whether it's better to vote yes or no, and answer with only "yes" or "no."

Let me weigh:

Key facts:
- No direct taxpayer cost (LAO verified) — this is the strongest point in favor. The downside risk to taxpayers is essentially nil; if the program fails to attract investors or borrowers, it just doesn't happen.
- The program is opt-in for homebuyers — nobody is forced to take the second mortgage. Those who take it presumably find it beneficial (or at least better than their alternatives, e.g., PMI or waiting years to save).
- It's tied to new construction, which addresses the classic criticism of demand-side subsidies (that they inflate prices of existing stock). Whether builders respond enough is uncertain, but even a partial supply response is better than subsidizing demand for existing homes.
- Broad coalition supports it: labor, business, taxpayer advocates claimed, Newsom, treasurer, controller, CTA, nurses, veterans, realtors, YIMBY cautiously.
- No formal opposition campaign even formed — opponents didn't submit a ballot argument.

Counterpoints:
- The League of Women Voters and several editorial boards raise legitimate concerns: opaque terms, second-mortgage burden, equity targeting, potential price inflation, sprawl.
- PPIC found most renters couldn't afford even entry-level new homes with the assistance; less than 40% of eligible renters could afford payments.
- The interest rates are unknown and could be high.

Assessment: The arguments against are mostly about the program being suboptimal, poorly targeted, or uncertain in impact — not about harm to taxpayers or the broader public. The arguments in favor emphasize it's a zero-taxpayer-cost experiment that could help tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of families and incentivize new construction. Given:
1. No taxpayer risk,
2. Voluntary participation,
3. Supply-side linkage,
4. Broad bipartisan/labor/business/housing-advocate support,
5. No organized opposition campaign,

...the reasonable conclusion leans toward "yes." The main risk is that it's ineffective, not that it's harmful. The SF Chronicle and SPUR endorsements align with this reasoning, and even critics like California YIMBY concede it's "a great idea in concept" with concerns about unintended consequences. The LAO says no direct costs. When a measure has no taxpayer cost, no mandatory state expenditure, is voluntary, and has no formal opposition, the case for trying it is stronger than the case for rejecting it.

However, I should seriously consider the "no" case: The League of Women Voters is a well-respected good-government group, and multiple editorial boards (Sac Bee, SD U-T, East Bay Times, Santa Cruz Sentinel, SLO Tribune) say no. Their core argument: it adds debt burden to families who may not be able to afford it; terms unknown; could inflate prices; equity concerns; sprawl.

But on balance — the proposition:
- Doesn't commit taxpayer money
- Creates a new financing tool administered by an existing, experienced agency (CalHFA)
- Requires annual independent audits
- Ties assistance to new construction (supply-positive)
- Has consumer protections (fixed rate, as-low-as-possible rates, hardship deferrals mentioned, no prepayment penalty)
- Is supported across the political spectrum

The strongest "no" arguments (unknown rates, investor interest, affordability of monthly payments) are real but are implementation risks that would be worked out by CalHFA; if the terms end up unattractive, borrowers simply won't use the program, and it costs the public nothing. The downside is bounded; the upside (potentially 60,000-1.8 million buyers helped, ~190,000 new homes) is significant in a state with a severe housing shortage and homeownership crisis.

I'll answer "yes."

3. Does it help people? Yes, potentially many families — voluntarily.
4. Is the program well-designed? Reasonably — with audits, caps, residency, occupancy requirements.
5. Opposition strength? No formal campaign; LWV and some editorials oppose.

Weighing bounded downside vs. meaningful upside, plus broad support from credible housing policy voices (SPUR, YIMBY cautiously, CalMatters neutral), "yes" is the better vote.

**Proposition 37 (California, November 2026): "Middle-Class Homeownership & Family Home Construction Act"**

Key facts:
- Authorizes up to $25B in *revenue bonds* (repaid by participating homebuyers, NOT taxpayers) for CalHFA to offer down-payment assistance loans (up to 17% of price) to middle-income CA residents buying newly constructed homes (price-capped ~$1M-$1.5M depending on county).
- LAO: No direct state or local costs. If investors don't buy bonds or borrowers don't participate, program simply doesn't scale.
- Broad support: Gov. Newsom, Treasurer Fiona Ma, Controller Malia Cohen, CA Democratic Party, unions (carpenters, nurses, teachers), chambers of commerce, CA Association of Realtors, veterans groups, YIMBY Action (cautiously), SPUR, SF Chronicle Editorial Board, LA Times' Skelton calls it a "no-brainer yes."
- Opposition: No formal ballot argument submitted, no opposition committee. League of Women Voters opposes (debt burden, unknown terms, equity targeting concerns). Several editorial boards (Sac Bee, SD U-T, East Bay Times/SLO, Santa Cruz Sentinel) recommend no — mainly on grounds it could inflate prices, add debt burden, be poorly targeted, and not address root supply/cost issues.
- Polls: PPIC September: 61% yes / 35% no; AIMSA October: 59% support.

Weighing the decision:

The "no" case rests on: (1) program design imperfections (not targeted to first-time buyers, high income caps), (2) uncertainty (rates, investor demand, actual impact), (3) concerns it could add debt burden to participating families or modestly inflate new-home prices, (4) it doesn't solve the root causes of high housing costs.

The "yes" case rests on: (1) zero direct taxpayer cost/risk — verified by LAO, (2) voluntary participation — families only take the second mortgage if it helps them, (3) uniquely supply-linked design (new construction only) that avoids the classic price-inflation failure mode of down-payment subsidies, (4) addresses a real, massive barrier (down payments of ~$180K on median homes), (5) consumer protections and audits built in, (6) broad bipartisan/labor/business/housing-advocate coalition, (7) bounded downside (if terms are unattractive, no one uses it and nothing is lost) vs. potentially large upside (60K-1.8M buyers potentially helped; possibly ~190K new homes).

The critical asymmetry: the downside risks are mostly borne voluntarily by participating borrowers and bond investors, not taxpayers or the general public. The program's flaws (poor targeting, unknown rates) mean it may be less effective than hoped, but effectiveness risks don't translate into public harm. Meanwhile, in a state with the second-worst homeownership rate and a severe housing shortage, a self-financing tool that channels demand into *new* construction is a defensible experiment. Even skeptical observers (California YIMBY, LA Times coverage) acknowledge the concept is good, with implementation concerns.

Given the bounded downside, zero taxpayer risk, voluntary nature, supply-side linkage, and broad support, "yes" is the better vote. Editorial boards split 2-2 per the California Today guide (though my count found more "no" editorials overall — Sac Bee, SD U-T, EB Times, SLO, Santa Cruz Sentinel vs. SF Chron; plus SPUR yes), but the analytical institutions that dug deepest (LAO, SPUR, PPIC, CalMatters) frame it as a low-risk, potentially beneficial experiment, and public polling shows strong support.

Final answer: yes

Buyers put 3% down, must occupy the home, and repay the loans — which repay the bonds.

**Key findings from my research:**
- **LAO confirms no direct taxpayer cost** — bonds are repaid by participating homebuyers, not the state; if investors or borrowers don't materialize, the program simply doesn't scale.
- **Unlike typical down-payment subsidies, it's tied to new construction only**, so the added demand lands where supply can respond — this addresses the classic price-inflation critique (a key reason the SF Chronicle editorial board and SPUR endorsed it).
- **Broad, cross-spectrum support:** Gov. Newsom, State Treasurer, State Controller, Democratic Party, labor unions (carpenters, nurses, teachers), chambers of commerce, Realtors, veterans groups, YIMBY advocates; ~61% in PPIC polling.
- **Criticism is real but mostly about suboptimality, not public harm:** League of Women Voters opposes it (second-mortgage debt burden, unknown rates/terms, weak equity targeting — no first-time-buyer priority, income caps up to ~$300K+); several editorial boards (Sac Bee, SD U-T, East Bay Times) say it won't solve root supply/cost problems; PPIC notes many eligible renters still couldn't afford even entry-level new homes.

**My assessment:** The downside is bounded and voluntary (borne by participating borrowers and bond investors, not taxpayers), while the potential upside — helping tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of families bridge a ~$180,000 down-payment hurdle while incentivizing new home construction in a state with the second-worst homeownership rate — is significant. No formal opposition even submitted a ballot argument or formed a committee. The flaws critics cite (targeting, unknown rates) would limit the program's *effectiveness*, not create taxpayer risk. On balance, the low-risk, supply-linked design makes this worth trying.

**yes**

PROP
37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
State Revenue Bonds. Bonds are a way that governments borrow money, most commonly for public projects such as schools or bridges. The state sells bonds to investors to receive up-front funding for these projects. Over time, investors are repaid with interest. The state sells two main types of bonds: general obligation bonds and revenue bonds. The state usually repays general obligation bonds using the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) In contrast, revenue bonds are repaid using revenue from fees or other payments by the users of the project (such as from bridge tolls).
Some People Seek Down Payment Assistance. When purchasing a home, most people pay some of the cost up front-typically 3 percent to 20 percent of the home price. The up-front payment is known as a down payment. If people cannot afford the down payment, there are different government programs available to provide down payment assistance to eligible homebuyers. To cover the remaining cost of the home, homebuyers get a loan, called a mortgage. Homebuyers then pay off the mortgage by making monthly payments that include interest.
California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA). CalHFA is a state entity that administers programs designed to help low- and moderate-income Californians afford housing. CalHFA has a few programs that provide down payment assistance to homebuyers. The down payment assistance programs are loans that must be repaid under certain terms and conditions.
Construction Defect Law. To try to prevent construction defects, state law sets minimum standards that builders must follow for new residential construction. Current law also establishes a process that homeowners and housing builders must follow before a homeowner is able to sue a builder for alleged violations of those minimum standards. For example, the homeowner must provide notice to the builder that includes certain information concerning a claim of construction defect.
PROPOSAL
Revenue Bond to Pay for a New Down Payment Assistance Program. Proposition 37 allows CalHFA to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. CalHFA would use the bond funds to create a down payment assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Each loan would cover up to 17 percent of the home price. (Homebuyers would need to provide a down payment of at least 3 percent of the home price.) Homeowners’ monthly payments on their loan would be designed to repay the bonds over time and cover the program’s administrative costs. CalHFA also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible. CalHFA would decide how much of the bonds to issue (up to $25 billion) and over what time period.
Buyers and Homes Must Meet Certain Requirements. To participate in a middleclass homeownership loan, people and homes would need to meet certain requirements. For example, an applicant would need to be a resident of the state and have a household income no more than double the typical income level in their area. For a home to be eligible for purchase through the program, among other requirements, the buyer would need to be the first purchaser of the home and the price could not exceed certain limits.
Housing Developer Options. Under Proposition 37, all developers could build homes eligible for purchase under the program. Developers also could choose to participate in a “qualified builder option.” Developers that chose this option would be required to meet higher labor standards, such as using workers with a certain type of training for certain types of housing projects. In exchange, developers would be subject to different construction defect rules, which generally aim to provide more flexibility to developers.
FISCAL EFFECTS
No Direct State or Local Costs. Because Proposition 37 uses the payments from homebuyers to repay bond investors, it would not result in direct state or local costs.
Other Potential Effects. A number of factors, which are unknown at this time, could affect Proposition 37’s scope and impact. These include (1) the extent to which investors want to buy the bond, (2) how much the loans available under this proposed program cost homebuyers compared with other down payment assistance options, and (3) whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying.

37

ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 37
VOTE YES ON PROPOSITION 37: the California Middle- Class Homeownership & Family Home Construction Act. Proposition 37 creates affordable homeownership opportunities for working and middle-class Californians and encourages new home construction-with ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS.
California has the second-worst homeownership rate in the nation; rising costs push homeownership further out of reach every year.
With the statewide median home price now exceeding $930,000, a traditional 20% down payment can require saving over $186,000 just to get in the door. Teachers, nurses, veterans, and firefighters work hard and pay their bills. They can afford monthly mortgage payments but are locked out of homeownership in the communities where they live and work because down payment requirements are too high.
Proposition 37 gives working and middle-class Californians a fair shot at homeownership.
KEEPING HOMEOWNERSHIP WITHIN REACH.
Prop. 37 is a practical solution. It makes consumer-friendly, low-interest downpayment assistance loans available to qualified California residents for purchasing a newly built home, with no cost to taxpayers.
This is not a handout. Homebuyers must qualify for a mortgage, meet income requirements, pay at least 3% down, occupy the home as their primary residence, make monthly payments, and fully repay their loans.
Prop. 37 is designed for renters, first-time homebuyers, and working families who earn too much to qualify for renter assistance programs, but not enough to save the massive down payment required to buy a home.
“Proposition 37 will boost homeownership without burdening taxpayers. As a state revenue bond, downpayment assistance loans are funded by private bond investors and repaid by home borrowers, not taxpayers.” -Malia Cohen, California State Controller
BUILDS MORE HOMES, CREATES GOOD JOBS.
California hasn’t built enough homes to keep up with demand. By helping qualified buyers purchase newly built homes, Prop. 37 will help accelerate construction, creating thousands of good-paying jobs and generating economic investment.
Expanding the housing supply helps workers and families to stay in California, build equity, raise their children, and live in the communities where they work.
ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS.
Taxpayer advocates and California’s Legislative Analyst agree: Proposition 37 has no cost to taxpayers. Loans are funded by private bond investors and repaid by home borrowers-not taxpayers.
STRICT ACCOUNTABILITY AND CONSUMER PROTECTIONS.
Prop. 37 includes fiscal accountability and transparency requirements, construction accountability standards, and annual audits detailing the status of loans made and the fund’s financial condition.
Consumer benefits include below-market, fixed-rate loans, protections from unfair lending practices, strict limits on lender fees, and no penalty for early repayment.
BROAD, BIPARTISAN SUPPORT
Proposition 37 is supported by Democrats & Republicans, labor and businesses, construction workers, taxpayer and housing advocates, veterans, the California Teachers Association, and United Nurses Association of California.
For generations, homeownership provided stability, security, and a path to the middle class. But today, that path is simply out of reach for too many Californians. Proposition 37 is a practical solution that tackles one of the biggest barriers to homeownership, without burdening taxpayers.
Vote YES to expand middle-class homeownership, build more homes, create good jobs, and give working Californians a fair chance to live, work, raise a family, and stay in California.
VoteYeson37.com
Danny Curtin , Director

California’s Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in down-payment loans for eligible middle-income buyers.
...
**The impact**
The ballot measure would allow qualified prospective homebuyers to borrow up to 17% of the sales price of a new home, contributing 3% of the down payment from their own funds.
The program would not be funded by taxpayers but instead by the interest charged to borrowers on their down-payment loans, also referred to as second mortgages.
Any home purchased through the program must be new construction, which could limit its potential reach because of the high cost of building.
The proposition does not spell out the terms or interest rates on the loans, which would be worked out if the measure was approved.
...
The measure has garnered widespread support, including from Gov.
Gavin Newsom, statewide unions and mayors from Santa Monica to San José.
Supporters say restricting the program to new homes could spur construction.
But critics warn down-payment debt could burden buyers and that Proposition 37 does little to address a bigger issue: the cost of building.

2. California propositions 2026: A quick guide to help you vote
https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Proposition 37: The measure would authorize the California Housing Finance Agency to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to help middle-income homebuyers.
The bonds would be repaid by homeowners' monthly loan and interest payments, not by taxpayers — to loan middle-income residents up to 17% of the cost of newly constructed houses, townhomes, row houses, condominiums and manufactured homes.
It aims to juice construction by eliminating red tape, particularly for condos.

Prop
37
CA
Prop
37
|
Bond
Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes
Authorizes $25 billion in state revenue bonds to encourage the construction of new homes and increase middle-class homeownership through second mortgages.
SPUR's Recommendation
SPUR supports the creation of new tools and financing to promote homeownership, and these revenue bonds would have no impact on the state’s General Fund. The focus on new construction will increase the supply of for-sale homes in the state and allow homebuyers to build generational wealth through home equity. While Prop. 37 could have focused more specifically on supporting populations that face barriers to homeownership, we believe its contribution to overall homeownership rates makes it worthy of support.
Vote YES
What Prop. 37 Would Do
Proposition 37 would authorize revenue bonds for fixed-rate second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, helping them afford a 20% down payment. Home loan borrowers would have to repay the bonds and administrative costs. The California Housing Finance Agency would offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of the purchase price of a newly constructed home. The bonds could not be used for existing homes. 1 Other requirements:
Homebuyers would have to make a minimum 3% down payment.
Second-mortgage loans would be limited to 17% of a home’s purchase price.
Homebuyers would put down 20% equity at purchase to eliminate the need for private mortgage insurance.
The maximum sales price for a qualified new home could not exceed 125% of the Federal Housing Finance Agency conforming loan limit for that county. (For example, the 2026 limit for San Francisco is $1,249,125; 125% of that limit would be $1,561,406).
Homebuyers would have to be California residents for at least one year and would agree to occupy the home as a primary residence.
Family income could not exceed 200% of the area median income (AMI) in the county or metropolitan statistical area where the new home is located.
The Backstory
The cost of housing in California has made homeownership increasingly challenging for many households, especially for Black and Latinx families who have experienced housing discrimination and have less inherited wealth, according to the Public Policy Institute of California. 2
This second-mortgage program would be available to households earning up to 200% of AMI, or $401,600 for a family of four in San Francisco.
Homeownership assistance has been a priority for former State Senator Bob Hertzberg. In 2022, he attempted to get a measure similar to Prop. 37 on the ballot through the state Legislature, but it failed. Former State Senator Anthony Portantino picked up the effort after Hertzberg was termed out of office, but he couldn't move legislation either. Hertzberg, now a private citizen, pivoted to a signature-gathering campaign and submitted more than 900,000 signatures this year to qualify Prop. 37 for the ballot. It requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
The racial equity impacts of Prop. 37 are unclear. While the Bay Area Equity Atlas found that the overall homeownership rate in the Bay Area is lower for Black (37%), Latinx (42%), and Native American (42%) households, this measure’s high cap of households earning up to 200% of AMI may disproportionately benefit Asian and white households, who have higher incomes and can more easily afford homeownership. In the Bay Area, the median income of Black and Latinx households is below 80% of AMI, according to U.S. Census data.
Pros
Prop. 37 would potentially create more homeownership opportunities in a state that, at 55.8%, has one of the lowest homeownership rates in the nation.
The measure focuses on new construction to increase housing supply rather than increasing demand for existing housing stock.
It would require the California Housing Finance Agency to conduct an independent annual audit of the program to ensure that bond proceeds are used in a manner consistent with the requirements.
Cons
Prop. 37 is not limited to first-time homebuyers and may therefore benefit Californians who could enter the market without its support.
The program is not targeted to low- or moderate-income households, allowing households with earnings of up to 200% of AMI to qualify. The maximum sales price may go up to 125% of the Federal Housing Finance Agency conforming loan limit.
Vote YES

Prop 37 endorsement: Buying a home in California can feel impossible. Is this the fix?
Most down-payment assistance programs for home buyers drive up housing costs. Prop 37 is different.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 15, 2026
It’s no secret that buying a home in California is a grim and mostly futile undertaking.
In the Bay Area, you need to make about $444,000 a year just to purchase a mid-priced home, according to a May report from the real estate brokerage Redfin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/realestate/article/home-buy-income-bay-area-22281201.php). A 2025 Zillow study found (https://www.sfchronicle.com/realestate/article/mortgage-rate-bay-area-20792146.php) that even if mortgage rates fell to 0%, most Bay Area families still couldn’t comfortably afford to buy.
Statewide, the median home price hovers around $900,000, according to the California Association of Realtors (https://carorg.sharepoint.com/:x:/s/CAR-RE-PublicProducts/IQAK-pU7cef4QpkWsCPlxwZKAbdKLa3OO0vFwHpuH_FADK8?rtime=9NSXc_YN30g). That puts a traditional 20% down payment out of reach for many families, locking them out of a pathway to generational wealth while simultaneously reducing the state’s political muscle as residents flee (https://www.ppic.org/blog/whos-leaving-california-and-whos-moving-in/) to cheaper, primarily red (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/housing-development-california-state-21027403.php), states.
Proposition 37 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot promises to help solve these problems by making it easier for middle-class Californians to enter homeownership.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The measure would permit the state to loan middle-income residents up to 17% of the cost of newly constructed houses, townhomes, row houses, condominiums and manufactured homes. Families with a traditional mortgage would only have to put 3% down.
Under Prop 37 in San Francisco, a family would need $40,000 for a median-priced home of about $1.3 million — compared to a 20% down payment of about $267,000.
Californians are clamoring for down payment help. When the state launched a down payment assistance program for first-time homebuyers in 2023, the $300 million on offer was spoken for in less than two weeks (https://www.sfchronicle.com/realestate/article/california-home-buyer-assistance-program-17888975.php).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But Prop 37 takes a different tack than traditional efforts like that one.
To start, it wouldn’t cost taxpayers a dime (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop37-110326.pdf).
The measure would authorize the California Housing Finance Agency to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds — which would be repaid by homeowners’ monthly loan and interest payments, not by taxpayers. Loan payments would also cover the administrative costs of the program, which will undergo an annual independent audit.
Nor will the measure drive up housing prices by subsidizing demand.
Only new homes explicitly constructed under the rules of the measure are eligible for Prop 37 loans. This incentivizes development instead of simply allowing more buyers to compete for a limited supply of existing homes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 37 aims to juice construction by eliminating red tape, particularly for condos.
Although condos are often the most affordable option for would-be homeowners, their production has fallen dramatically in California due to the state’s “right to repair” law, which effectively encourages homeowners to sue developers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/condo-home-california-law-22306098.php) for alleged construction defects — even easily fixable ones that aren’t harmful.
This year, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, attempted a fix with a bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB1903) that would have comprehensively overhauled California’s right-to-repair law.
But it died in the final moments of the legislative session (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/09/condo-construction-bill-dies/?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=WhatMatters&utm_source=31&npnl=NTA2MTM0fDc4YTAyODgwNzMxZGY1NThiZTI5MGVlZGUxOTA2Y2VhYzNlNTFlMGM3YTJkYTNhNjZiNzFhZTljYzM1Njg5ODM&utm_source=ActiveCampaign&utm_medium=email&utm_content=Is%20Gavin%20Newsom%20in%20his%20lame%20duck%20era%3F&utm_campaign=WhatMatters) — even after being significantly watered down.
Prop 37 would reanimate some aspects of Wicks’ bill.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It would require claimants to clearly specify each alleged violation and permit them to release builders from liability if repairs are completed satisfactorily. It also incentivizes quick resolution of lawsuits — builders could ask courts to dismiss actions against them if claimants drag their feet — and caps attorneys’ fees at 30% of total recovery.
With legislative reform in limbo, “the condo defect implications of Prop 37 are solid,” Leora Tanjuatco Ross, YIMBY Action’s California director, told the editorial board.
We certainly hope that lawmakers pursue more transformative defect reform in the future. But until that happens, Prop 37 could serve as a stopgap.
The ability of middle-class buyers to finance a home, such as these along Kirkwood Avenue in San Francisco, seen on April 9, 2022, would be enhanced with the passage of S.F.’s Prop 37 in November.
Justin Katigbak/For the S.F. Chronicle The measure also requires builders who want to take advantage of these right-to-repair reforms to meet certain labor standards, such as providing workers’ compensation and unemployment insurance, while abiding by state and local laws requiring prevailing wage — or union-level pay — for large-scale projects.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Those who have lived in California for at least a year and have a family income of 80% to 200% of the area median income — which in San Francisco ranges from about $104,000 to $260,000 for a family of two (https://media.api.sf.gov/documents/2026_AMI-IncomeLimits-HMFA.pdf) — are eligible for Prop 37 loans.
No, you can’t use Prop 37 for a second home; qualifying homes must be the buyer’s primary residence. Eligible home prices are capped, too — they can’t be sold for more than 125% of the conforming loan limit for a one-unit property in the county in question, which is about $1.5 million in San Francisco.
The measure also contains consumer protections. For instance, it requires the program’s mortgage loans to be fixed-rate and instructs the California Housing Finance Agency to set them “as low as possible.” It also permits the agency to establish a homeowner education requirement.
Just how affordable these loans would be, however, is an open question. As a California Budget Center analysis noted (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/will-proposition-37-make-homeownership-more-affordable-its-not-guaranteed/#h-how-is-prop-37-different-from-california-s-existing-downpayment-assistance-programs), the Housing Finance Agency’s loans may come with higher-than-usual interest rates because they’re second mortgages. Investors view these as riskier than first mortgages, which are repaid first if a homeowner defaults.
Former state Sen. Bob Hertzberg, a Democrat from Los Angeles County who collected signatures to put Prop 37 on the ballot, told the editorial board that he believes the measure could create 190,000 homes and spur $150 billion in economic activity.
That certainly sounds transformative. But is the measure likely to live up to Hertzberg’s hype?
Prop 37 has no formal opposition and most experts we spoke with were cautiously supportive.
The measure technically didn’t need to go to the ballot; the Legislature or housing finance agency could have established the program. We’re not a fan of politicians using the ballot for their vanity projects, and there’s certainly some ego at play for Hertzberg, who referred to the homes that could be built under Prop 37 as “Hertzberg houses.”
But Hertzberg did try to get the Legislature to approve a version of the program (https://shou.senate.ca.gov/sites/shou.senate.ca.gov/files/7.%20SB%201457%20%28Hertzberg%29%20-%20analysis.pdf), to no avail.
“I’m just a burnt-out old politician trying to do the right thing who hasn’t lost his soul, and I might help the motherf—ers in the middle class if I die doing it,” said Hertzberg, who clearly subscribes to the John Burton school of profanity. (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/john-burton-obituary-17820175.php)
About Opinion
The editorial positions of The Chronicle, including election recommendations, represent the consensus of the editorial board , consisting of the publisher, the editorial page editor and staff members of the opinion pages. Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
Prop 37’s scope is limited enough that we don’t think it will fundamentally change California’s housing landscape. But given how dire our housing crisis is, any positive impact is better than none at all.
We recommend a yes vote.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Buying a home in California requires a colossal amount of money — and coming up with a 20% cash down payment of $180,000 for a median price home is a staggering hurdle for many would-be buyers.
That down payment amount is based on the statewide median $900,000 price tag for a house, according to recent data from (https://www.car.org/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/sept2026sales) the California Assn. of Realtors. In Los Angeles County, the median price for a single-family home is $935,000. In Orange County, it’s $1.5 million.
Proposition 37 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-37-loans-middle-class-homeowners-voter-guide) on the Nov. 3 ballot would allow the state to amass a $25 billion down payment assistance program for middle-class households. For perspective on the enormity of the measure before voters, one of the state’s existing down payment programs, California Dream For All, launched several years ago with $500 million, just 2% of the funding involved in Proposition 37.

The ballot measure would allow qualified prospective homebuyers to borrow up to 17% of the sales price of a new home, contributing 3% of the down payment from their own funds.
The program would not be funded by taxpayers, but instead by the interest charged to borrowers on their down payment loans, also referred to as second mortgages. The measure has garnered widespread support, including from Gov. Gavin Newsom, statewide unions and mayors from Santa Monica to San José.
“Prop. 37 is a historic opportunity to expand homeownership opportunities for generations of working families — at zero cost or risk to taxpayers,” Newsom said in a statement.

But Proposition 37 carries a significant caveat: Any home purchased through the program must be new construction, which could limit its potential reach because of the high cost of building, some critics said.
Also, the proposition does not spell out the terms or interest rates on the loans, which would be worked out if the measure is approved. And some have questioned whether there will be sufficiently robust interest from investors to buy the state-issued bonds that will be used to fund the down payment loans.
The concept of down payment assistance is not new. Cities and states, including California, have long offered such programs to low- and middle-income homeowners, either in the form of loans or grants, and there are reportedly more than 2,700 such programs (https://downpaymentresource.com/professional-resource/down-payment-assistance-continues-to-expand-in-q1-2026-reaching-2679-programs-nationwide/) across the country.
Nevada, Connecticut, Massachusetts and New York all have programs to help homebuyers afford a down payment. Since 2021, New York has dispersed $70 million (https://www.ncsha.org/hfa-news/new-york-state-homes-and-community-renewal-announces-major-milestones-in-expanding-access-to-affordable-homeownership/) in down payment assistance. In Massachusetts, more than $146 million has been doled out in down payment help to homebuyers since 2020.
How the program would work
Under Proposition 37, down payment loans would work like any other, and would carry an interest rate and payback period — all of which would be determined by the California Housing Finance Agency.
To qualify, borrowers would need to have lived in the state for at least a year and earn no more than 200% of the local median income; in Los Angeles County, for example, that equates to a family of four earning no more than $216,200 a year.

While Proposition 37 has little opposition, and is supported by unions, chambers of commerce and organizations representing builders, the League of Women Voters opposes the ballot measure (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/), concerned it would saddle residents with too much debt and that the terms of these loans are opaque, the details worked out only after the vote.
New homes only
Only buyers of newly-built homes would be eligible for these loans. That could include existing commercial buildings that had been converted into homes, such as condos or townhomes.
This provision is uncommon as many existing down payment assistance programs don’t strictly limit the type of home someone can buy — only the sale price. Bob Hertzberg, former Senate Majority Leader and the architect of the proposal, said he wanted Proposition 37 to spur new construction.
“The problem is we have to increase supply,” Hertzberg said. The shortage of homes (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-09-27/how-bad-is-californias-housing-shortage-it-depends-on-whos-doing-the-counting) in the state is estimated to range anywhere from 840,000 (https://upforgrowth.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/2024_Housing-Underproduction-in-the-U.S.-Report_Final-c-1.pdf) to upwards of 3 million. (https://www.mckinsey.com/~/media/mckinsey/industries/public%20and%20social%20sector/our%20insights/closing%20californias%20housing%20gap/closing-californias-housing-gap-full-report.pdf)

By creating more demand for new homes, he said, the hope is that builders will respond en masse.
But some groups are wary of this logic. One analysis (https://voteyeson37.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Prop-37-Homeownership-Analysis-1.pdf), funded by the Proposition 37 campaign, estimated that this program could result in the building of 190,000 homes in the state, although the report’s author said it was “impossible to know” the true number given the various factors that impact housing.
Matthew Lewis, director of communications for California YIMBY, an organization that advocates making it easier and cheaper to build homes, said high prices make it clear that the demand for homes already exists and that Proposition 37 does little to address a bigger issue: the cost of building.

“In concept, [Proposition 37 is] a great idea,” Lewis said. “The thing we’re concerned about is, California is still way behind on its housing production goals, so there’s the risk of an unintended consequence of instead of having 10 people bidding on a house, now you’ve given a couple folks down payment assistance, and so there’s now 12 people bidding on the same house.”
To drive builders to construct eligible homes, the measure would allow them to opt into a “qualified builder” option. As long as they adhere to price caps, agree to certain labor requirements and fix repairs that arise, they’re protected from lawsuits from buyers concerning defects 10 years after construction of the home.
Homebuilders say even given some relief from litigation, they aren’t sure Proposition 37 would push construction into overdrive.
Advertisement
“There are so many more things the state, city and county could do to help add more supply [of homes],” said Paul Schon, a developer who builds apartments in L.A. County. He said tackling permitting times and red tape involved in building would have a greater impact. “This is minor,” he said.
Interest rates could be a tough sell
Many down payment assistance programs offer interest-free loans to homebuyers, including an existing program run by CalHFA.
But in order to be self-funding, the fixed-rate loans offered through Proposition 37 would carry interest. If passed, the state would issue revenue bonds, selling them to investors and using that money to issue loans to homebuyers. The investors are repaid with the interest paid on the loans.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026), CalHFA would decide the total amount of bonds to issue and over what period of time.
Revenue bonds are generally viewed as riskier than other types of government bonds, in part because they’re backed by the promise of revenue from a specific project (https://www.msrb.org/Sources-Repayment) — in this case, payment by individual borrowers. That means interest rates on these loans could be higher than borrowers might like or be able to afford.
Hertzberg said he’s talked to investors who may be willing to buy these bonds at cheaper rates, given the crushing issue the funding is trying to solve. This would keep interest rates down for borrowers. He said he’s appealing to foundations and socially-minded tech leaders.

One of the biggest financial backers of the measure is the political nonprofit Building a Better California, which has been fighting the billionaire’s tax with help from wealthy donors (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax), including Google co-founder Sergey Brin.
Hertzberg, for his part, refused to name any organization or person who may be interested in buying the bonds that would fund this program.

Will Prop. 37 Make Homeownership More Affordable? It’s Not Guaranteed
Understanding How Proposition 37 Could Affect Homeownership Affordability
August 2026 | By Monica Davalos (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/monica-davalos/), Nishi Nair (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/nishi-nair/), and Kristin Schumacher (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kristin-schumacher/)
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 37 on the November 2026 ballot would establish a “middle-class” homebuyer downpayment assistance program, funded with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. This assistance could only be used to purchase newly built homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser. The program is intended to be self-sustaining because participating homebuyers — not the state — would ultimately repay the bonds through their mortgage payments.
